country.name: Kazakhstan
country.tagline: Vineyards under the Tian Shan east of Almaty, where a young estate industry buries its vines each winter.

stats.note: Small wine sector; no reliable vineyard total found.

country.overview: Kazakhstan is the world's largest landlocked country, but almost all of it is too cold or too dry for vines. Its wine country lies in the far south-east, in the foothills of the Zailiysky Alatau (Tian Shan) east of Almaty, and in the south around Shymkent and the Turkestan region. Soviet planners established large vineyards here; many were lost after 1985 and 1991. Since the late 2000s private estates have replanted the Almaty region, most visibly Arba Wine in the Enbekshikazakh district towards Shelek and Turgen, with others nearby. Winters are severe enough that vines are buried in autumn and dug out in spring, and summers are hot and dry with irrigation from mountain rivers. Kazakhstan is also an important market for Georgian and Moldovan wine.

history.title: State vineyards in the south
history.text: Soviet planners planted vineyards in the Almaty and Shymkent regions, many of them lost after the 1985 anti-alcohol campaign and independence.

history.title: Private estates east of Almaty
history.text: New wineries such as Arba Wine replanted the foothills east of Almaty.

country.climate_soils: Extreme continental, 600 to 1,000 metres, vines buried in winter, irrigated loess and alluvial fans.

grapes.name: Saperavi, Rkatsiteli, Cabernet Sauvignon, Riesling, Chardonnay

sites.text: The foothills of the Zailiysky Alatau east of Almaty around Shelek and Turgen, where Kazakhstan's new estates (including Arba Wine) grow vines that must be buried each winter.
